chief_complaint: severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting in a pregnant patient
hpi_details: A 28-year-old female presents to the clinic with severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting; she is currently pregnant. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening.
ideas: She thinks the intense pain under her ribs is severe acid reflux or delayed morning sickness caused by the growing baby pressing against her stomach.
concerns: She is terrified that the severe abdominal pain and fever might harm her unborn baby or trigger premature labor.
expectations: She hopes to have an ultrasound to confirm that her baby's heartbeat is safe and to receive pregnancy-safe medicine to relieve the pain and nausea.

investigation_events.title: Urgent pregnancy-safe cholecystitis workup
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent laboratory and right-upper-quadrant ultrasound results are now available; pregnancy-safe fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, and specialist consultation should not be delayed.

results.value: Gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening to 5 mm, trace pericholecystic fluid, and positive sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 4 mm

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Cholecystitis in Pregnancy evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Cholecystitis in Pregnancy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes performing an RUQ ultrasound, starting IV fluids and pregnancy-safe antibiotics, and consulting OB/GYN and surgery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Cholecystitis in Pregnancy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Biliary colic without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain in pregnancy — needs urgent assessment given risk to both mother and baby.
management_principles: Perform RUQ ultrasound, start IV fluids, safe antibiotics, consult OB/GYN and surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.plan: Perform an RUQ ultrasound (preferred imaging in pregnancy) and start IV fluids with pregnancy-safe antibiotics. Consult OB/GYN and surgery jointly given the risk to both mother and fetus; escalate promptly if symptoms worsen.

teaching.one_liner: Pregnancy hormones make bile thicker and gallstones more likely; when a stone blocks the gallbladder, it becomes inflamed, causing right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and vomiting.
red_flags: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain in pregnancy — needs urgent assessment given risk to both mother and baby

must_ask.say: How many weeks pregnant are you?
Did the pain start after a fatty meal?
Does the pain spread to your shoulder blade or your back?
Have you had a fever or chills?
Have you noticed the baby moving normally?
Have you been told before that you have gallstones?

history.answer: I'm pregnant, and I've been having this terrible pain in my upper right belly along with a fever and throwing up.
The pain started around yesterday evening, maybe 18 hours ago, and it has been gradually getting worse.
It is mainly in the upper right side of my stomach, right under my ribs, and it hasn't shifted anywhere else.
Yes, the pain radiates around to my right shoulder blade and the right side of my back.
It's a constant, deep, severe ache that occasionally throbs, rather than coming and going in waves.
Right now it is an 8 out of 10, and it has definitely become much more intense since last night.
It felt a lot worse after I ate dinner last night, and deep breaths or moving around also aggravate it. Nothing really relieves it.
About two hours before the pain started, I ate fried chicken for dinner. I haven't had any alcohol.
I've had a couple of milder stomach aches after greasy foods over the past few months, but nothing ever this severe or lasting this long.
I've been feeling nauseous and threw up three times since last night. It was mostly stomach fluid and yellowish bile, no blood.
Yes, I checked my temperature at home earlier this morning and it was 38.1 degrees Celsius, and I had shivers.
My bowel movements have been normal, no diarrhea, and I'm still passing gas. I haven't seen any blood or black or pale stools.
No, my skin and eyes look normal, and my urine hasn't turned dark or tea-colored.
No pain or burning when I pee, and I haven't noticed any blood in my urine.
No, I haven't felt faint or dizzy, even when standing up.
No vaginal bleeding, spotting, or unusual discharge at all.
No chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath, other than it hurting to take a very deep breath.
I'm currently 20 weeks pregnant with my first baby.
Yes, I've felt the baby moving normally today, just like usual.
No, I've never been told I had gallstones, and I haven't had an abdominal ultrasound before.
I thought this terrible pain under my ribs was just really bad acid reflux or delayed morning sickness from the baby crowding my stomach.
I'm so scared that this high fever and uncontrollable vomiting will hurt my baby or cause me to go into early labor.
I really hope you can do a quick scan to make sure my baby is safe and give me something pregnancy-safe to stop this pain and vomiting.
I've always been healthy without any chronic medical illnesses like hypertension or diabetes.
I've never had any surgeries or hospital stays before.
I only take my daily prenatal vitamins and folic acid. I haven't taken any NSAIDs, aspirin, or painkillers.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I used to have an occasional drink socially, but I completely stopped drinking alcohol once I found out I was pregnant.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband.
My mother had her gallbladder removed in her forties because of gallstones, but no other major illnesses in the family.
Before becoming pregnant my periods were regular every 28 days, and my last menstrual period was about 20 weeks ago.
No heart rhythm issues, palpitations, or vascular diseases.

exam.finding: Alert, visibly uncomfortable and guarding her right upper abdomen, but in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 102 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, body temperature 38.1°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are pink without pallor.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without crackles or wheezes.
Tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Gravid abdomen consistent with second trimester; no surgical scars, visible distension, or caput medusae.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard in all four quadrants; no abdominal bruits.
Tympanitic throughout except dullness over the right upper quadrant; no shifting dullness.
Marked focal tenderness and involuntary guarding in the right upper quadrant; left side and lower abdomen are soft without tenderness.
Mild localized rebound tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no generalized peritonitis.
Inspiratory arrest upon deep palpation beneath the right costal margin.
No tenderness at McBurney's point; negative psoas and obturator signs.
No lower extremity edema or calf tenderness bilaterally.
